draft.title: Opposition to the war
card: As the war went on, many people in the United States and Australia came to oppose their country's part in it. Protests grew through the late 1960s and early 1970s.
Conscription

Both countries used conscription, which meant young men could be called up to fight. In Australia, men were chosen by a birthdate ballot. Many people objected to young men being forced to fight in a war they did not support.
Casualties
Rising numbers of dead and wounded soldiers, and news coverage of the fighting on television, made the cost of the war clear to people at home.
Moratorium marches
In 1970, large Moratorium marches were held in Australian cities, including Melbourne and Sydney. Thousands of people marched to call for an end to Australia's involvement.
draft.remember: Conscription and casualties turned many people against the war, and the 1970 Moratorium marches showed that opposition in Australia.

a.q: Which of these helped to make opposition to the war grow in Australia and the United States?
opts: Young men being conscripted and rising casualties
The communists winning the 1968 election in Saigon
Governments ending conscription at the start of the war
The war being fought close to Australian cities
a.why: Conscription meant young men could be forced to fight, and rising casualties showed the cost of the war. Together these made many people at home oppose it. The other options describe events that did not happen.
a.clue: Think about what the war asked of young men and families at home.

b.q: In 1970, thousands of people marched through Melbourne and Sydney in the Moratorium marches. What did the marches show?
opts: Many Australians wanted an end to involvement in the war
Most Australians wanted to send more troops to Vietnam
Australians were protesting against the end of conscription
Australians were protesting only about local taxes
b.why: The marches were a public call to end Australia's involvement in the war, so they showed growing opposition. The option about sending more troops is wrong because the marchers were calling for the opposite.
b.clue: Ask what the marchers wanted to happen to Australia's role in the war.

a.best: Young men being conscripted and rising casualties

b.best: Many Australians wanted an end to involvement in the war

problems.detail: The distractors are plainly absurd for Year 12 HSC students: the war was not fought near Australian cities, there was no conscription ending at the start, and there was no 1968 communist election win in Saigon. The question tests almost nothing.

The distractors are obviously wrong ('only about local taxes', 'more troops', 'against the end of conscription'), so the question is too easy for Year 12 and barely tests understanding of the Moratorium.

proposal.title: Opposition to the war
card: At first, most Australians supported the war and conscription. Through the late 1960s, opposition grew in both Australia and the United States.
Conscription

Both countries conscripted young men, meaning the government could make them serve. From 1965, Australia chose 20-year-olds by a birthdate ballot and could send them to Vietnam, though the voting age was then 21.
Casualties
As deaths and wounds mounted, television news brought the fighting into homes each night. The deaths of conscripts made the war's cost feel especially close.
Moratorium

In May 1970, Moratorium marches drew tens of thousands in Melbourne and large crowds in other cities, calling for troops to come home. Workers, parents and older people marched with students, showing opposition had spread well beyond campuses.
proposal.remember: Conscription and casualties turned a once-supportive public against the war, and the 1970 Moratorium showed how wide that opposition had become.

a.q: By 1970, far more Australians opposed the war than in 1965. Which best explains this change?
opts: Mounting casualties, including conscripts sent to Vietnam
The Moratorium marches, which began the debate in 1965
Conscription being brought in for the first time in 1970
Less television coverage of the fighting at home
a.why: Rising deaths, made vivid by nightly television news and felt sharply when conscripts died, turned many people against the war. The Moratorium is tempting, but it was held in 1970, so it was a sign of growing opposition rather than its starting cause.
a.clue: Look for a cause that was already at work between 1965 and 1970.

b.q: A historian argues that by 1970, opposition to the war had spread beyond radical students. Which evidence best supports this?
opts: Workers, parents and older people marched with students
Students had protested on university campuses for years
Most Australians backed the war and conscription in 1965
Conscripts were chosen by a birthdate ballot from 1965
b.why: The claim is about who opposed the war, so the best evidence shows people other than students protesting, as happened in the 1970 Moratorium. Campus protests are tempting, but they show only that students opposed the war, not that opposition had spread wider.
b.clue: The evidence must show who was protesting, not just that protests happened.

a.best: Mounting casualties, including conscripts sent to Vietnam

b.best: Workers, parents and older people marched with students
